# Hypothesis: an __exit__ annotated to return bool may swallow exceptions, so the statement after the with-block stays reachable when the body raises, while an __exit__ returning None does not.
from typing import reveal_type
from types import TracebackType


class Swallow:
    def __enter__(self) -> int:
        return 41

    def __exit__(
        self,
        exc_type: type[BaseException] | None,
        exc: BaseException | None,
        tb: TracebackType | None,
    ) -> bool:
        return exc_type is ValueError


class Keep:
    def __enter__(self) -> str:
        return "ok"

    def __exit__(
        self,
        exc_type: type[BaseException] | None,
        exc: BaseException | None,
        tb: TracebackType | None,
    ) -> None:
        return None


def run_swallow(flag: bool) -> str:
    with Swallow() as value:
        reveal_type(value)
        if flag:
            raise ValueError("boom")
    return "after block"


def run_keep(flag: bool) -> str:
    with Keep() as text:
        reveal_type(text)
        if flag:
            return "early"
    return "fell through"


_swallow = Swallow()
_keep = Keep()
assert run_swallow(True) == "after block"
assert run_swallow(False) == "after block"
assert run_keep(True) == "early"
assert run_keep(False) == "fell through"
hypothesis: An __exit__ annotated to return bool may swallow exceptions, so code after the with-block stays reachable when the body raises, unlike an __exit__ returning None.
